name: Ontological argument
definition: An a priori deductive argument that God's existence follows from the definition of God alone.
precision_note: A priori and deductive — it appeals to no observation at all. This is what separates it from design and cosmological.
interacts_with: A priori; Necessary existence; Lost island
presented_by: Anselm of Canterbury (Benedictine monk, 1033–1109) — "that than which nothing greater can be conceived"
attack_1: Kant (Philosopher, 1724–1804) argues that existence is not a predicate, so it cannot count as a perfection.
attacker_1: Immanuel Kant (Philosopher, 1724–1804) — "Being is evidently not a real predicate"
defence_1: Plantinga (Analytic philosopher, 1932–) reformulates the argument modally, in terms of necessary existence in all possible worlds.
attack_2: Gaunilo replies that the same reasoning would establish the existence of a perfect island, which is absurd.
attacker_2: Gaunilo of Marmoutiers (Benedictine monk, c. 994–1083) — "the lost island"
defence_2: Anselm answers that only God has necessary existence; an island is contingent by nature, so the parody does not apply.
defender_2: Anselm of Canterbury (Benedictine monk, 1033–1109) — "that than which nothing greater can be conceived"

name: A priori
definition: Known independently of experience, by analysing concepts alone.
precision_note: Contrast a posteriori. Only the ontological argument is a priori; design and cosmological are a posteriori.

name: A posteriori
definition: Known through experience and observation of the world.
precision_note: Design and cosmological are both a posteriori, which is why both are vulnerable to empirical counter-explanation.

name: Greatest conceivable being
aka: That than which nothing greater can be conceived
definition: Anselm's definition of God as the being no greater than which can be thought.
precision_note: Not 'the greatest being that exists' — that would assume the conclusion. It is a definition of the concept.

name: Existence in intellectu and in re
aka: In the mind and in reality
definition: Anselm's distinction between existing only as an idea and existing in reality.
precision_note: The argument turns on the claim that in re is greater than in intellectu alone.

name: Necessary existence
definition: Existence that could not have failed to obtain; a being that cannot not exist.
precision_note: Anselm's second form. Distinguish from contingent existence, and from logical necessity of propositions.

name: Lost island objection
definition: Gaunilo's parody: the same reasoning would define a perfect island into existence.
precision_note: Anselm's reply is that only God has necessary existence; islands are contingent, so the parody fails.

name: Existence is not a predicate
definition: Kant's objection that existence adds nothing to a concept, so it cannot be a perfection.
precision_note: Saying a thing exists says how many there are, not what it is like. This is the strongest ontological objection.

name: Design argument
definition: An a posteriori argument from apparent order and purpose in nature to a designer.
precision_note: Distinguish design qua purpose (Paley) from design qua regularity, and both from modern fine-tuning.
presented_by: William Paley (Anglican archdeacon, 1743–1805) — "the watch must have had a maker"
attack_1: Hume (Philosopher, 1711–1776) argues the analogy between the universe and a machine is too weak to support the conclusion.
defence_1: Swinburne (Philosopher of religion, 1934–) replies that the argument is inductive and cumulative, not a strict analogy.
attack_2: Darwin (Naturalist, 1809–1882) shows that apparent design in organisms arises from variation and differential survival.
defence_2: Defenders relocate the argument from biology to the fine-tuning of physical constants.
attack_3: Hume (Philosopher, 1711–1776) argues that even a successful argument would not establish the God of classical theism.
defence_3: The argument is one strand of a cumulative case, not a proof of the full doctrine of God on its own.
attack_4: Calvin (Reformer, 1509–1564) holds that fallen reason cannot reach God from nature unaided.
defence_4: Aquinas (Dominican friar, c. 1225–1274) holds reason wounded but not destroyed by the Fall, so natural theology remains possible.
attack_5: The design argument delivers at most a designer, not the Trinitarian creator of Christian doctrine.
defence_5: The arguments work cumulatively toward theism, with revelation supplying the specifically Christian content.

name: Watch analogy
definition: Paley's comparison: finding a watch on a heath implies a watchmaker, so contrivance in nature implies a contriver.
precision_note: The force is in contrivance — parts arranged for a purpose — not mere complexity.

name: Contrivance
definition: Parts adapted and put together for an end.
precision_note: Paley's actual criterion. Students often say 'complexity', which is weaker and easier to attack.

name: Analogy
definition: Inference from resemblance between two things to further resemblance.
precision_note: Analogical arguments are only as strong as the relevant similarity. This is the hinge of the Hume dispute.

name: Weak analogy objection
definition: Hume's claim that the universe is unlike a machine, and is a single case with no comparison class.
precision_note: We have observed many watches being made and no universes, so the inductive base is empty.

name: Epicurean hypothesis
definition: Hume's suggestion that given infinite time, random arrangements of matter would eventually produce apparent order.
precision_note: Order does not require a designer if chance has unlimited trials.

name: Natural selection
definition: Darwin's mechanism by which apparent design arises from variation and differential survival.
precision_note: Defeats biological design but leaves cosmological fine-tuning untouched. Say which one you mean.

name: Anthropic principle
definition: The claim that the physical constants are improbably suited to life, suggesting design.
precision_note: The modern successor to Paley. The multiverse is the standard reply.

name: Cosmological argument
definition: An a posteriori argument from the existence or contingency of the universe to a necessary being.
precision_note: AQA specifies Way 3 (contingency and necessity), not Ways 1 and 2. Do not substitute the argument from motion.
presented_by: Thomas Aquinas (Dominican friar, c. 1225–1274) — "it is necessary to admit a first efficient cause"
attack_1: Russell (Philosopher, 1872–1970) charges the argument with the fallacy of composition.
attacker_1: Bertrand Russell (Philosopher, 1872–1970) — "the universe is just there, and that's all"
defence_1: Copleston (Jesuit priest, 1907–1994) replies that the question of the series as a whole is legitimate and demands sufficient reason.
attack_2: Hume (Philosopher, 1711–1776) denies that we can reason from causation within the universe to a cause of the universe.
defence_2: Aquinas (Dominican friar, c. 1225–1274) argues from dependence rather than from temporal causation, so Hume's point misses the target.
attack_3: An infinite chain of contingent causes would remove the need for a necessary being.
defence_3: Aquinas (Dominican friar, c. 1225–1274) rejects an infinite regress of dependent causes, not an infinite series of events.
defender_3: Thomas Aquinas (Dominican friar, c. 1225–1274) — "it is necessary to admit a first efficient cause"

name: Contingency
definition: The property of being able not to exist; depending on something else for existence.
precision_note: Aquinas's Way 3 turns on everything contingent having a time it did not exist.

name: Infinite regress
definition: An unending chain of causes or explanations with no first member.
precision_note: Aquinas rejects it as explaining nothing; Russell and Hume see no problem in it.
attack_1: An infinite chain of contingent causes would remove the need for a necessary being.
defence_1: Aquinas (Dominican friar, c. 1225–1274) rejects an infinite regress of dependent causes, not an infinite series of events.
defender_1: Thomas Aquinas (Dominican friar, c. 1225–1274) — "it is necessary to admit a first efficient cause"

name: Principle of sufficient reason
definition: Everything that exists has an explanation of its existence.
precision_note: Copleston's premise. Russell simply denies it, which is why the debate stalls there.
attack_1: Russell (Philosopher, 1872–1970) denies that the universe requires any explanation at all.
attacker_1: Bertrand Russell (Philosopher, 1872–1970) — "the universe is just there, and that's all"
defence_1: Refusing the question is not answering it; a brute fact is an admission that the explanation is unavailable.

name: Fallacy of composition
definition: Wrongly inferring that what is true of every part is true of the whole.
precision_note: Russell's objection: every human has a mother, the human race does not.

name: Brute fact
definition: Something that exists with no further explanation.
precision_note: Russell's position on the universe. It is a refusal of the question, not an answer to it.

name: Problem of evil
definition: The difficulty of reconciling the existence of evil with an omnipotent, omnibenevolent God.
precision_note: Always specify logical or evidential — they need different replies.
presented_by: Epicurus (Philosopher, 341 BC–270 BC) — "Is he willing to prevent evil, but not able?"

name: Natural evil
definition: Suffering caused by natural processes rather than human choice.
precision_note: The free will defence handles moral evil directly and natural evil only indirectly. That gap is examinable.
attack_1: The defence addresses moral evil but leaves natural suffering unexplained.
defence_1: Soul-making covers natural evil where the free will defence cannot.

name: Moral evil
definition: Suffering caused by the deliberate choices of free agents.

name: Logical problem of evil
definition: The claim that God and evil are strictly incompatible, so theism is incoherent.
precision_note: A deductive claim. One coherent theodicy defeats it, which is why Plantinga's defence is enough.
interacts_with: Inconsistent triad; Evidential problem of evil

name: Evidential problem of evil
definition: The claim that the amount and distribution of evil makes God improbable rather than impossible.
precision_note: Harder to answer than the logical version, because a merely possible defence does not lower the improbability.
attack_1: Calling suffering an absence does not lessen it.
defence_1: Privation explains the origin of evil, not its severity, and was never offered as consolation.
defender_1: Augustine of Hippo (Bishop of Hippo Regius, 354–430) — "privation of good"

name: Inconsistent triad
definition: Mackie's claim that omnipotence, omnibenevolence and the existence of evil cannot all be true.
precision_note: Any solution must deny or qualify one leg. Identify which leg each theodicy weakens.
presented_by: J.L. Mackie (Philosopher, 1917–1981) — "the inconsistent triad"
attack_1: Christian doctrine affirms all three of the propositions Mackie (Philosopher, 1917–1981) says cannot be held together.
defence_1: The free will defence shows the three propositions are not strictly inconsistent.
defender_1: Alvin Plantinga (Analytic philosopher, 1932–) — "the free will defence"

name: Omnipotence
definition: The property of being all-powerful.
precision_note: Often qualified rather than denied — 'cannot do the logically impossible' is the standard move.
attack_1: A God who cannot guarantee the outcome departs from classical theism.
defence_1: Classical omnipotence is itself a philosophical accretion rather than a biblical necessity.

name: Omnibenevolence
definition: The property of being wholly good.

name: Privatio boni
definition: Augustine's view that evil is not a substance but an absence of the good that should be present.
precision_note: If evil is not a thing, God did not create it. The objection is that absences still cause real suffering.
presented_by: Augustine of Hippo (Bishop of Hippo Regius, 354–430) — "privation of good"
attack_1: Calling suffering an absence does not lessen it.
defence_1: Privation explains the origin of evil, not its severity, and was never offered as consolation.
defender_1: Augustine of Hippo (Bishop of Hippo Regius, 354–430) — "privation of good"

name: Theodicy
definition: An attempted justification of God in the face of evil.
precision_note: A theodicy claims to give the actual reason; a defence claims only a possible one. Plantinga offers a defence.

name: Soul-making theodicy
definition: Hick's view that the world is designed for moral and spiritual growth, not comfort.
precision_note: Humans are made in God's image and must grow into His likeness. Requires universal salvation to be just.
presented_by: John Hick (Philosopher of religion, 1922–2012) — "a vale of soul-making"
attack_1: The scale and distribution of suffering exceeds anything growth could require.
defence_1: Hick (Philosopher of religion, 1922–2012) argues that suffering must be genuinely excessive and unfairly distributed to do its work.
defender_1: John Hick (Philosopher of religion, 1922–2012) — "a vale of soul-making"

name: Epistemic distance
definition: The cognitive gap between God and humans that leaves room for free faith.
precision_note: If God were obvious, response would be compelled rather than free. Central to Hick.

name: Universal salvation
definition: The view that all people are ultimately saved.
precision_note: Hick needs this: soul-making is unjust if some suffer and are then lost anyway.

name: Free will defence
definition: The claim that genuine free will necessarily allows the possibility of evil, and is worth its cost.
precision_note: A defence, not a theodicy. Mackie's reply: God could have made agents who always freely choose good.
attack_1: Mackie (Philosopher, 1917–1981) replies that God could have created agents who always freely choose the good.
defence_1: A world of agents who always freely choose good may not be feasible for God to actualise.
attack_2: The defence addresses moral evil but leaves natural suffering unexplained.
defence_2: Soul-making covers natural evil where the free will defence cannot.
defender_2: John Hick (Philosopher of religion, 1922–2012) — "a vale of soul-making"

name: Process theodicy
definition: Griffin's view that God is not omnipotent but works by persuasion within an uncreated universe.
precision_note: Solves evil by denying omnipotence outright. The cost is a God who may lose.
presented_by: David Ray Griffin (Process theologian, 1939–2022)
attack_1: A God who cannot guarantee the outcome departs from classical theism.
defence_1: Classical omnipotence is itself a philosophical accretion rather than a biblical necessity.
attack_2: A God who is neither omnipotent nor creator departs from the Christian doctrine of God.
defence_2: Process theology preserves God's goodness, which the creeds treat as more central than omnipotence.

name: Persuasive power
definition: God influences by luring rather than coercing.

name: Dipolar God
definition: Whitehead's God with both an unchanging primordial nature and a changing consequent nature.
precision_note: Allows God to suffer with creation — 'a fellow sufferer who understands'.

name: Religious experience
definition: An encounter taken by the subject to be of, or from, the divine.
precision_note: Classify before you evaluate: vision, numinous, or mystical. Each is challenged differently.
attack_1: Psychological and neurological accounts explain religious experience without reference to any object.
defence_1: A causal story about how an experience arises does not show there was nothing to experience.
attack_2: Freud (Neurologist, 1856–1939) argues religious experience is wish fulfilment arising from an infantile need for a protective father.
defence_2: Swinburne (Philosopher of religion, 1934–) replies that a causal account of how a belief arises does not show it false.
attack_3: Persinger (Cognitive neuroscientist, 1945–2018) argues religious experiences are produced by temporal lobe activity.
defence_3: Swinburne (Philosopher of religion, 1934–) replies that a neural correlate is what one would expect either way.

name: Corporeal vision
definition: A vision in which the figure is seen with the physical eyes, external to the subject.

name: Imaginative vision
definition: A vision seen in the mind, as in a dream or trance.

name: Intellectual vision
definition: An insight or awareness with no sensory content at all.
precision_note: Hardest to challenge on neurological grounds, since there is nothing sensory to explain away.

name: Numinous
definition: Otto's term for the non-rational apprehension of the holy as wholly other.
precision_note: Note it is an experience of otherness and creatureliness, not union. The opposite of mystical unity.
presented_by: Rudolf Otto (Lutheran theologian, 1869–1937) — "the wholly other"
attack_1: Otto (Lutheran theologian, 1869–1937) describes encounter with radical otherness; Stace (Philosopher, 1886–1967) describes union without distinction.
defence_1: Otto (Lutheran theologian, 1869–1937) and Stace (Philosopher, 1886–1967) describe different stages rather than rival essences of religious experience.

name: Mysterium tremendum et fascinans
definition: The holy as simultaneously terrifying and compelling.

name: Wholly other
definition: God as radically unlike anything in creation.
precision_note: Otto uses it experientially; it also supports the via negativa in religious language.

name: Mystical experience
definition: A non-sensuous, non-intellectual union with the divine.
precision_note: Union, not encounter. This is the structural contrast with Otto's numinous.
presented_by: William James (Psychologist, 1842–1910) — "ineffable, noetic, transient, passive"
attack_1: Otto (Lutheran theologian, 1869–1937) describes encounter with radical otherness; Stace (Philosopher, 1886–1967) describes union without distinction.
defence_1: Otto (Lutheran theologian, 1869–1937) and Stace (Philosopher, 1886–1967) describe different stages rather than rival essences of religious experience.

name: Ineffability
definition: The quality of being beyond adequate description in words.
precision_note: One of James's four marks. Cuts both ways: it also blocks verification.
attack_1: If mystical states cannot be described, they cannot be reported in a way testimony can transmit.
defence_1: Ineffability limits description, not communication; the reports are of a recognisable type.

name: Noetic quality
definition: The sense that the experience conveys genuine knowledge, not just feeling.

name: Transiency
definition: The brevity of mystical states.

name: Passivity
definition: The sense of being acted upon rather than acting.

name: Undifferentiated unity
definition: Stace's introvertive mysticism: awareness of unity with no distinctions at all.
precision_note: Stace's cross-cultural claim; the objection is that reports are shaped by prior belief.

name: Principle of credulity
definition: Swinburne's rule that things are probably as they seem unless there is reason to doubt.
precision_note: Shifts the burden of proof onto the sceptic. That shift is what critics attack.
presented_by: Richard Swinburne (Philosopher of religion, 1934–) — "the principle of credulity"
attack_1: Swinburne's default trust and the reductionist default suspicion cannot both govern the same reports.

name: Principle of testimony
definition: Swinburne's rule that we should normally believe what others report.
attack_1: If mystical states cannot be described, they cannot be reported in a way testimony can transmit.
defence_1: Ineffability limits description, not communication; the reports are of a recognisable type.

name: Defeaters
definition: Conditions under which credulity or testimony can be overridden.
precision_note: Swinburne lists them; the debate is whether religious experience routinely meets them.

name: Wish fulfilment
definition: Freud's claim that religion projects an infantile longing for a protective father.
precision_note: A genetic account: it explains the origin, not the truth. That is the standard reply.

name: Neurological reductionism
definition: The claim that religious experiences are brain states with natural causes.
precision_note: Correlation is not causation — a neural correlate is what you would expect either way.

name: Symbol
definition: Tillich's view that religious language participates in the reality it points to.
precision_note: A symbol differs from a sign: it shares in what it signifies. The objection is that this is unverifiable.
presented_by: Paul Tillich (Lutheran theologian, 1886–1965) — "ultimate concern"
attack_1: There is no way to establish whether a symbol genuinely participates in what it points to.
defence_1: Symbols are tested by whether they still disclose ultimate concern, not by empirical check.

name: Ultimate concern
definition: Tillich's term for what a person takes as unconditionally important; his description of God.

name: Analogy of attribution
definition: Aquinas's view that qualities are ascribed to God as their cause.

name: Analogy of proportion
definition: Aquinas's view that a quality belongs to God in proportion to God's nature.
precision_note: Both analogies avoid univocal and equivocal language. Name which one you mean.
presented_by: Thomas Aquinas (Dominican friar, c. 1225–1274) — "analogy of proportion"
attack_1: Pure negation and analogy give incompatible accounts of how much can be said.
defence_1: Analogy and negation operate together: the via negativa clears the ground that analogy then occupies.
defender_1: Thomas Aquinas (Dominican friar, c. 1225–1274) — "analogy of proportion"

name: Univocal language
definition: Using a word in exactly the same sense of God and creatures.
precision_note: Risks anthropomorphism.

name: Equivocal language
definition: Using a word in a wholly different sense of God.
precision_note: Risks meaninglessness. Analogy is Aquinas's middle way between the two.

name: Via negativa
definition: Speaking of God only by denial, saying what God is not.
precision_note: Protects transcendence at the cost of content. Ask whether pure negation says anything at all.
attack_1: Pure negation and analogy give incompatible accounts of how much can be said.
defence_1: Analogy and negation operate together: the via negativa clears the ground that analogy then occupies.
defender_1: Thomas Aquinas (Dominican friar, c. 1225–1274) — "analogy of proportion"

name: Cataphatic way
definition: Speaking of God positively, by affirmation.

name: Cognitive language
definition: Language that makes factual claims capable of truth or falsity.
precision_note: The whole debate is whether religious statements are cognitive. Settle that before evaluating.
attack_1: Ayer (Philosopher, 1910–1989) argues religious statements are factually meaningless because they cannot be verified.
defence_1: Hick (Philosopher of religion, 1922–2012) argues religious statements are verifiable in principle after death.
attack_2: Flew (Philosopher, 1923–2010) argues believers will not say what would count against their claims, so the claims assert nothing.
attacker_2: Antony Flew (Philosopher, 1923–2010) — "death by a thousand qualifications"
defence_2: Hare (Moral philosopher, 1919–2002) replies that bliks are unfalsifiable but meaningful because they shape how one lives.
attack_3: Insulating religious language from outside criticism also cuts it off from outside support.
defence_3: Losing outside support is no loss if outside support was never available anyway.
defender_3: Ludwig Wittgenstein (Philosopher, 1889–1951) — "the meaning of a word is its use"

name: Non-cognitive language
definition: Language that expresses attitude, commitment or intention rather than fact.
precision_note: Hare, Wittgenstein and arguably Tillich are non-cognitivist. Believers often reject the label.

name: Verification principle
definition: The logical positivist claim that a statement is meaningful only if analytic or empirically verifiable.
precision_note: Self-refuting: the principle is neither analytic nor verifiable. Always available as a counter.
spec_codes: CH01; CH03; CH04; ET08; PH08; PH09
attack_1: Non-natural moral properties cannot be verified empirically.
defence_1: Verificationism is self-refuting, so its failure to accommodate moral facts is not decisive against them.
attack_2: There is no way to establish whether a symbol genuinely participates in what it points to.
defence_2: Symbols are tested by whether they still disclose ultimate concern, not by empirical check.

name: Falsification principle
definition: Flew's claim that an assertion is meaningful only if something could count against it.
precision_note: Stronger than verification because it targets the believer's refusal to specify counter-evidence.
interacts_with: Death by a thousand qualifications; Blik

name: Death by a thousand qualifications
definition: Flew's charge that believers erode a claim by qualifying it until it asserts nothing.

name: Blik
definition: Hare's term for an unfalsifiable but meaningful way of seeing the world.
precision_note: Bliks are meaningful because they matter and guide action, not because they are true.

name: Eschatological verification
definition: Hick's claim that religious statements are verifiable in principle after death.
precision_note: Keeps religious language cognitive. The objection: verification only one way, and only if you survive.
interacts_with: Verification principle; Parable of the Celestial City

name: Language game
definition: Wittgenstein's view that meaning is determined by use within a rule-governed form of life.
precision_note: Protects religious language from outside criticism, but at the price of insulating it from outside support.
attack_1: Insulating religious language from outside criticism also cuts it off from outside support.
defence_1: Losing outside support is no loss if outside support was never available anyway.
defender_1: Ludwig Wittgenstein (Philosopher, 1889–1951) — "the meaning of a word is its use"

name: Form of life
definition: The shared practice within which a language game has its sense.

name: Miracle
definition: An event of religious significance, variously defined as a violation of natural law or as a natural event given meaning.
precision_note: Definition decides the argument. State which you are using in the first sentence.
interacts_with: Violation of natural law; Anti-realist view of miracle
attack_1: Wiles (Anglican priest, 1923–2005) argues that a God who intervenes selectively would be arbitrary and unjust.
attacker_1: Maurice Wiles (Anglican priest, 1923–2005) — "one single act of creation"
defence_1: Selective action is no more arbitrary than answered prayer, which most believers already accept.
attack_2: Reported miracles can be explained as misperception, coincidence or later embellishment.

name: Violation of natural law
definition: Hume's definition of a miracle as a transgression of a law of nature by a deity.
precision_note: Loads the dice: laws are defined by uniform experience, so evidence against is always maximal.
attack_1: Hume's definition makes the conclusion inevitable.
defence_1: Even granting the definition is contested, the practical argument about witnesses stands independently.
defender_1: David Hume (Philosopher, 1711–1776) — "a violation of the laws of nature"

name: Realist view of miracle
definition: A miracle is an objective event that actually happened in the world.
attack_1: The anti-realist account preserves the language while abandoning the claim believers make.
defence_1: Believers assert that something happened, and the creeds stake everything on the resurrection.

name: Anti-realist view of miracle
definition: A miracle is an event whose significance lies in its meaning for a community.
precision_note: Lets the account survive scientific challenge, but critics say it empties the claim.
attack_1: The anti-realist account preserves the language while abandoning the claim believers make.
defence_1: Believers assert that something happened, and the creeds stake everything on the resurrection.
attack_2: A God who acts in history is presupposed by the creeds, so purely symbolic miracle undercuts the doctrine.
defence_2: Anti-realists argue the theological meaning was always the point, even for the earliest communities.

name: Hume's argument against miracles
definition: Testimony is never strong enough to establish a miracle, since the improbability always exceeds the witness's reliability.
precision_note: Two strands: an argument in principle, and practical points about witnesses and rival religions.
presented_by: David Hume (Philosopher, 1711–1776) — "a violation of the laws of nature"
attack_1: Hume's definition makes the conclusion inevitable.
defence_1: Even granting the definition is contested, the practical argument about witnesses stands independently.
defender_1: David Hume (Philosopher, 1711–1776) — "a violation of the laws of nature"

name: Testimony
definition: Reported evidence from witnesses.
precision_note: Hume attacks its quality; Swinburne defends it in the religious experience topic. Useful synoptic link.
interacts_with: Hume's argument against miracles; Principle of testimony

name: Single act of creation
definition: Wiles's view that God acts once in creating and sustaining, not by particular interventions.
precision_note: Motivated by justice: selective intervention would make God arbitrary. The cost is a God who never acts now.
presented_by: Maurice Wiles (Anglican priest, 1923–2005) — "one single act of creation"
attack_1: A God who never acts particularly is hard to square with scripture and with prayer.

name: Arbitrariness objection
definition: If God intervenes at Lourdes but not at Auschwitz, God is unjust.
precision_note: Links miracles directly to the problem of evil. A strong synoptic paragraph.
interacts_with: Single act of creation; Problem of evil

name: Substance dualism
definition: The view that mind and body are two distinct substances.
precision_note: Descartes's position. The interaction problem is the standard objection.
presented_by: Rene Descartes (Philosopher, 1596–1650) — "I think, therefore I am"
attack_1: Ryle (Philosopher, 1900–1976) argues dualism is a category mistake, treating the mind as a thing of the same kind as the body.
attacker_1: Gilbert Ryle (Philosopher, 1900–1976) — "the ghost in the machine"
defence_1: Ryle's charge presupposes materialism rather than establishing it.
defender_1: Rene Descartes (Philosopher, 1596–1650) — "I think, therefore I am"
attack_2: Two immaterial and material substances cannot causally interact without explanation.
defence_2: Hylomorphism dissolves the interaction problem without collapsing into materialism.
defender_2: Aristotle (Philosopher, 384 BC–322 BC) — "the soul is the form of the body"
attack_3: Christian orthodoxy raises the embodied person; Descartes' surviving soul makes resurrection unnecessary.
defence_3: Resurrection and dualism can be combined: the soul persists and is reunited with a raised body.

name: Materialism
definition: The view that only physical substance exists; mental states are physical states.
precision_note: Makes survival of death depend on bodily resurrection, not an immortal soul.
attack_1: Two immaterial and material substances cannot causally interact without explanation.
defence_1: Hylomorphism dissolves the interaction problem without collapsing into materialism.
defender_1: Aristotle (Philosopher, 384 BC–322 BC) — "the soul is the form of the body"

name: Cogito
definition: Descartes's claim that the certainty of thinking establishes the self as a thinking thing.
precision_note: Establishes that I exist as a thinker; the leap to a separate substance is the disputed step.

name: Hylomorphism
aka: Soul as form of the body
definition: Aristotle's view that the soul is the form of the body, not a separate substance.
precision_note: Neither dualism nor materialism. Aquinas adopts it, which complicates 'Christianity is dualist'.
presented_by: Aristotle (Philosopher, 384 BC–322 BC) — "the soul is the form of the body"
attack_1: If the soul is the form of the body, it does not obviously survive the body's destruction.
defence_1: Aquinas (Dominican friar, c. 1225–1274) holds the rational soul subsists after death and is completed by resurrection.

name: Category mistake
definition: Ryle's charge that dualism treats the mind as a thing of the same kind as the body.
precision_note: Like asking to see the university after seeing all the colleges.
interacts_with: Ghost in the machine; Substance dualism

name: Ghost in the machine
definition: Ryle's mocking description of the Cartesian soul.

name: Resurrection
definition: Continued existence through the raising of an embodied person.
precision_note: Christian orthodoxy is resurrection of the body, not immortality of the soul. Students routinely conflate them.
interacts_with: Immortality of the soul; Replica theory
presented_by: Augustine of Hippo (Bishop of Hippo Regius, 354–430)
attack_1: Greek immortality and biblical resurrection are different doctrines with different implications.
defence_1: Christian tradition absorbed Plato (Philosopher, c. 428 BC–348 BC)nic language while keeping resurrection as the substantive doctrine.
defender_1: Augustine of Hippo (Bishop of Hippo Regius, 354–430)
attack_2: Christian orthodoxy raises the embodied person; Descartes' surviving soul makes resurrection unnecessary.
defence_2: Resurrection and dualism can be combined: the soul persists and is reunited with a raised body.
attack_3: If there is no separable soul, there is no bearer of identity between death and resurrection.
attacker_3: Gilbert Ryle (Philosopher, 1900–1976) — "the ghost in the machine"
defence_3: Hick (Philosopher of religion, 1922–2012) argues God can recreate the person, with continuity of pattern securing identity.
attack_4: Process thought preserves the person only as everlasting memory in God, not as a continuing subject.
defence_4: Objective immortality abandons personal survival, which process thought regards as a lesser loss than divine coercion.

name: Immortality of the soul
definition: Continued existence of a non-physical soul after bodily death.
precision_note: Platonic rather than biblical. Distinguish it from resurrection.
presented_by: Plato (Philosopher, c. 428 BC–348 BC) — "the body is the prison of the soul"
attack_1: If the soul is the form of the body, it does not obviously survive the body's destruction.
defence_1: Aquinas (Dominican friar, c. 1225–1274) holds the rational soul subsists after death and is completed by resurrection.
attack_2: Greek immortality and biblical resurrection are different doctrines with different implications.
defence_2: Christian tradition absorbed Plato (Philosopher, c. 428 BC–348 BC)nic language while keeping resurrection as the substantive doctrine.
defender_2: Augustine of Hippo (Bishop of Hippo Regius, 354–430)

name: Replica theory
definition: Hick's thought experiment that an exact recreated person would be the same person.
precision_note: Defends resurrection against the identity objection. Critics say a replica is a copy, not you.
presented_by: John Hick (Philosopher of religion, 1922–2012)
attack_1: A replica appears to be a copy rather than the original person.
defence_1: The duplication objection describes a case God would have no reason to bring about.

name: Personal identity
definition: What makes someone the same person over time.
precision_note: The real question behind afterlife debates. Bodily continuity, memory, or soul.

name: Natural moral law
definition: Aquinas's deontological theory that moral rules are derived by reason from human nature and its God-given purpose.
precision_note: Deontological and absolutist, but with a teleological foundation in purpose. Say both.
spec_codes: AP01; AP02; CH11; CH12; CH13; CH16; CH17; ET01; ET02
presented_by: Thomas Aquinas (Dominican friar, c. 1225–1274) — "good is to be done and evil avoided"
attack_1: Hume's is-ought gap denies that any conclusion about what ought to be follows from what is.
defence_1: Defenders argue NML is more flexible than its critics allow.
attack_2: Allowing proportionate reasons arguably makes the theory consequentialist.
defence_2: Double effect already allows outcomes to matter without making the theory consequentialist.
defender_2: Thomas Aquinas (Dominican friar, c. 1225–1274) — "good is to be done and evil avoided"
attack_3: Fletcher (Episcopal priest, 1905–1991) rejects the exceptionless precepts that NML derives from human purpose.
defence_3: Secondary precepts are fallible and context-sensitive, so NML is less rigid than Fletcher (Episcopal priest, 1905–1991) assumes.
defender_3: Thomas Aquinas (Dominican friar, c. 1225–1274) — "good is to be done and evil avoided"
attack_4: Liberation theology begins from the experience of the oppressed rather than from a fixed rational order.
attack_5: The spec's own contrast: a theory ordered to natural ends and a lived reality it excludes.

name: Eternal law
definition: God's rational ordering of the universe, known fully only to God.

name: Divine law
definition: The part of eternal law revealed in scripture.

name: Natural law
definition: The part of eternal law knowable by human reason.
precision_note: This is why NML is available to non-believers — a strength worth citing.

name: Human law
definition: Particular laws made by societies, valid only if consistent with natural law.

name: Primary precepts
definition: The five basic goods: preserve life, reproduce, educate, live in society, worship God.
precision_note: Absolute and universal. The secondary precepts derived from them are where disagreement lives.

name: Secondary precepts
definition: Specific rules reasoned out from the primary precepts.
precision_note: Fallible, because reason can err. This is the flexibility in NML students often miss.

name: Synderesis
definition: The innate disposition to do good and avoid evil.
precision_note: Aquinas's synderesis rule. Appears in both NML and conscience — a ready synoptic link.

name: Real and apparent good
definition: A real good genuinely fulfils human purpose; an apparent good only seems to.
precision_note: Explains wrongdoing as error rather than malice.

name: Doctrine of double effect
definition: An act with a good intended effect may be permissible even if it has a foreseen bad effect.
precision_note: Requires the bad effect to be foreseen but not intended, and not the means to the good.

name: Proportionalism
definition: The view that one may go against a precept if there is a proportionate reason.
precision_note: A modification of NML, not a separate theory. Critics call it consequentialism in disguise.
interacts_with: Natural moral law; Doctrine of double effect
attack_1: Allowing proportionate reasons arguably makes the theory consequentialist.
defence_1: Double effect already allows outcomes to matter without making the theory consequentialist.
defender_1: Thomas Aquinas (Dominican friar, c. 1225–1274) — "good is to be done and evil avoided"

name: Telos
definition: The end, purpose or goal of a thing.
precision_note: Shared by NML and virtue ethics. Do not treat 'teleological' as a synonym for 'consequentialist'.

name: Situation ethics
definition: Fletcher's teleological theory that the loving thing is the right thing in each situation.
precision_note: Not 'do whatever you feel'. Agape is a disposition of will, not an emotion.
presented_by: Joseph Fletcher (Episcopal priest, 1905–1991) — "love is the only absolute"
attack_1: Fletcher (Episcopal priest, 1905–1991) rejects the exceptionless precepts that NML derives from human purpose.
defence_1: Secondary precepts are fallible and context-sensitive, so NML is less rigid than Fletcher (Episcopal priest, 1905–1991) assumes.
attack_2: Setting aside biblical commands in the name of love subordinates God's revealed will to human judgement.
defence_2: Fletcher (Episcopal priest, 1905–1991) argues Jesus himself set aside law for love, so agape is the biblical principle.
defender_2: Joseph Fletcher (Episcopal priest, 1905–1991) — "love is the only absolute"
attack_3: Agape is directed at persons, so animal welfare enters only through its effect on people.

name: Agape
definition: Selfless, unconditional love that wills the neighbour's good.
precision_note: The only intrinsic good for Fletcher. Everything else is instrumental.

name: Four working principles
definition: Pragmatism, relativism, positivism and personalism.
precision_note: Positivism is the key one: the commitment to love is chosen, not proved.

name: Six propositions
definition: Fletcher's six statements setting out how agape functions as the sole norm.

name: Legalism
definition: Rule-following applied without regard to circumstance.
precision_note: One of Fletcher's two rejected extremes.

name: Antinomianism
definition: Acting with no rules or principles at all.
precision_note: Fletcher's other rejected extreme. Situationism is the middle way.

name: Virtue ethics
definition: Aristotle's character-based theory concerned with what sort of person to be rather than what to do.
precision_note: Agent-centred, not act-centred. That is why 'it gives no guidance in a dilemma' is the standard objection.
spec_codes: AP01; AP02; CH11; CH12; CH13; CH17; ET03
presented_by: Aristotle (Philosopher, 384 BC–322 BC) — "the mean relative to us"
attack_1: Virtue ethics is agent-centred where Kant (Philosopher, 1724–1804) is act-centred.
defence_1: Practical wisdom supplies the guidance in particular cases that a rule could not anticipate.
attack_2: Virtue ethics gives no clear guidance in a dilemma.
defence_2: Aristotle (Philosopher, 384 BC–322 BC)'s practical wisdom is precisely the capacity to judge particular cases.

name: Eudaimonia
definition: The final end for humans: living and doing well, a whole-life flourishing.
precision_note: Not 'happiness' as pleasure. It is an activity, not a feeling.

name: Golden mean
definition: Virtue lies between excess and deficiency, relative to the person and situation.
precision_note: Not an arithmetic average. Some acts have no mean at all.

name: Moral virtue
definition: A settled disposition of character acquired by habit.

name: Intellectual virtue
definition: An excellence of thought acquired by teaching.

name: Phronesis
definition: The intellectual virtue of judging rightly what to do in particular cases.
precision_note: Aristotle's answer to the 'no guidance' objection.

name: Habituation
definition: Becoming virtuous by repeatedly performing virtuous acts.
precision_note: We become just by doing just acts — the circularity is deliberate.

name: Practice and tradition
definition: MacIntyre's revival of virtue within socially embedded practices with internal goods.
precision_note: Useful for showing virtue ethics is a live theory, not only ancient.

name: Utilitarianism
definition: The teleological theory that the right act maximises pleasure and minimises pain.
precision_note: A naturalistic meta-ethical position: it defines good in terms of a natural property.
spec_codes: CH10; CH17; ET04; ET05; ET06; ET08
presented_by: Jeremy Bentham (Jurist, 1748–1832) — "nature has placed mankind under two sovereign masters"
attack_1: Moore (Philosopher, 1873–1958) charges utilitarianism with the naturalistic fallacy in defining good as pleasure.
defence_1: Moore's argument shows only that 'good' resists definition, not that pleasure fails to track it.
defender_1: Jeremy Bentham (Jurist, 1748–1832) — "nature has placed mankind under two sovereign masters"
attack_2: Utilitarianism permits injustice to individuals when the sum works out.
defence_2: Rule utilitarianism blocks the punishment of innocents, since a rule permitting it would reduce utility.
defender_2: Jeremy Bentham (Jurist, 1748–1832) — "nature has placed mankind under two sovereign masters"
attack_3: An intrinsic and equal value cannot be traded off against aggregate welfare.
attack_4: Liberation theology prioritises the poor as a matter of justice, not because it maximises aggregate welfare.

name: Principle of utility
definition: Acts are right in proportion as they promote happiness.

name: Hedonic calculus
definition: Bentham's seven criteria for measuring pleasure: intensity, duration, certainty, propinquity, fecundity, purity, extent.
precision_note: Quantitative only. Mill's higher and lower pleasures is the reply to its crudeness.
attack_1: Ranking pleasures by quality imports a standard outside pleasure itself.
defence_1: Competent judges who have experienced both pleasures are still judging by preference, not by an external standard.

name: Act utilitarianism
definition: Each individual act is judged by its own consequences.
precision_note: Flexible but can license appalling individual acts.

name: Rule utilitarianism
definition: Rules are adopted which, generally followed, maximise utility.
precision_note: Strong rule utilitarianism collapses toward deontology; weak collapses back into act.

name: Higher and lower pleasures
definition: Mill's distinction between intellectual and bodily pleasures, with the former qualitatively superior.
precision_note: Answers the 'philosophy of swine' charge but arguably imports a non-utilitarian standard.
attack_1: Ranking pleasures by quality imports a standard outside pleasure itself.
defence_1: Competent judges who have experienced both pleasures are still judging by preference, not by an external standard.
defender_1: John Stuart Mill (Philosopher, 1806–1873) — "better a human being dissatisfied than a pig satisfied"

name: Preference utilitarianism
definition: The right act best satisfies the preferences of those affected.
precision_note: Singer's version. Extends easily to animals via sentience.

name: Kantian ethics
definition: Kant's theory that morality is a matter of duty determined a priori by reason.
precision_note: Consequences are morally irrelevant. This is the sharpest contrast with Bentham.
presented_by: Immanuel Kant (Philosopher, 1724–1804) — "act only on that maxim you can will universal"
attack_1: Virtue ethics is agent-centred where Kant (Philosopher, 1724–1804) is act-centred.
defence_1: Practical wisdom supplies the guidance in particular cases that a rule could not anticipate.
attack_2: Kantian absolutism produces monstrous results in extreme cases.
defence_2: Kant's murderer case turns on what you may be held responsible for, not on indifference to outcome.
defender_2: Immanuel Kant (Philosopher, 1724–1804) — "act only on that maxim you can will universal"
attack_3: Kant's postulate of God and immortality reintroduces reward into a supposedly autonomous ethic.
defence_3: The summum bonum is a postulate of practical reason, not a motive for acting.
defender_3: Immanuel Kant (Philosopher, 1724–1804) — "act only on that maxim you can will universal"

name: Categorical imperative
definition: A command binding unconditionally, regardless of desire.
precision_note: Three formulations. Universal law and ends in themselves are the two AQA needs.

name: Hypothetical imperative
definition: A command binding only if you want a particular end.
precision_note: Kant's contrast class. Moral commands are never hypothetical.

name: Universalisability
definition: Act only on a maxim you could will to become a universal law.
precision_note: Tests for contradiction in conception or in will, not for bad consequences.

name: Ends in themselves
definition: Treat humanity never merely as a means but always also as an end.
precision_note: Merely' matters. Using someone is permitted; using them only as a tool is not.

name: Kingdom of ends
definition: The ideal community in which all treat each other as ends.

name: Good will
definition: The only thing good without qualification: acting from duty alone.
precision_note: Acting in accordance with duty is not enough; it must be from duty.

name: Duty
definition: The necessity of acting from respect for the moral law.

name: Autonomy and heteronomy
definition: Autonomy is self-legislation by reason; heteronomy is being governed by outside authority.
precision_note: Why Kant sits awkwardly with divine command theory. A strong dialogue point.
attack_1: Kant's autonomy is incompatible with morality grounded in obedience to a command.
defence_1: God's commands may express the rational moral order rather than override it.

name: Summum bonum
definition: The highest good: virtue rewarded with happiness.
precision_note: Kant's postulate of God and immortality. A back door to religion in a supposedly autonomous ethic.
attack_1: Kant's postulate of God and immortality reintroduces reward into a supposedly autonomous ethic.
defence_1: The summum bonum is a postulate of practical reason, not a motive for acting.
defender_1: Immanuel Kant (Philosopher, 1724–1804) — "act only on that maxim you can will universal"

name: Divine command theory
definition: Right is what God commands and wrong is what God forbids.
precision_note: Meta-ethical: it defines moral terms, it is not merely a decision procedure.
attack_1: Kant's autonomy is incompatible with morality grounded in obedience to a command.
defence_1: God's commands may express the rational moral order rather than override it.
attack_2: Either an act is good because God commands it, making morality arbitrary, or God commands it because it is good, making morality independent of God.
defence_2: God's nature, not an arbitrary decree, is the standard, so neither horn bites.
attack_3: DCT defines moral terms by reference to a divine will rather than a natural property.
defence_3: Divine commands can be understood as tracking natural human goods rather than replacing them.

name: Euthyphro dilemma
definition: Is an act good because God commands it, or commanded because it is good?
precision_note: Either morality is arbitrary or God is subject to an external standard. The central objection to DCT.

name: Voluntarism
definition: The view that God's will alone determines morality.
precision_note: Takes the first horn of Euthyphro and accepts the arbitrariness.

name: Meta-ethics
definition: The study of the meaning and status of moral language rather than of what is right.
precision_note: Second-order. A question about 'good' itself, not about which acts are good.

name: Ethical naturalism
definition: Moral properties are natural properties, so moral statements are verifiable facts.
precision_note: Utilitarianism is the AQA example: good is defined as pleasure.
attack_1: Intuitions conflict between people and cultures with no way to adjudicate.
defence_1: Disagreement is about the non-moral facts of cases, not about the simple property of goodness.
attack_2: DCT defines moral terms by reference to a divine will rather than a natural property.
defence_2: Divine commands can be understood as tracking natural human goods rather than replacing them.

name: Ethical non-naturalism
definition: Moral properties are real but not natural, and are known by intuition.
precision_note: Intuitionism is the AQA example.

name: Intuitionism
definition: Moral values are self-evident and known directly, not derived or defined.
precision_note: Moore holds good is simple and indefinable, like yellow.
presented_by: G.E. Moore (Philosopher, 1873–1958) — "the naturalistic fallacy"
attack_1: Non-natural moral properties cannot be verified empirically.
defence_1: Verificationism is self-refuting, so its failure to accommodate moral facts is not decisive against them.
attack_2: Intuitions conflict between people and cultures with no way to adjudicate.
defence_2: Disagreement is about the non-moral facts of cases, not about the simple property of goodness.

name: Naturalistic fallacy
definition: Moore's charge that defining good in terms of any natural property is a mistake.
precision_note: Distinct from Hume's is-ought gap, though they are usually run together. Note the difference.

name: Is-ought gap
definition: No statement of what ought to be follows validly from statements of what is.
precision_note: Hume's version. Threatens NML, which derives ought from human nature.

name: Open question argument
definition: For any natural definition of good, 'but is it good?' remains a sensible question.
precision_note: Moore's support for the naturalistic fallacy.

name: Cognitivism and non-cognitivism in ethics
definition: Whether moral statements state facts or express attitudes.
precision_note: The same distinction as in religious language. A clean synoptic bridge.

name: Free will
definition: The capacity to choose otherwise than one did.
precision_note: Define it before arguing; libertarians and compatibilists mean different things by it.
attack_1: Calvin's decree of election threatens responsibility from a theological direction.
defence_1: Predestination concerns God's eternal knowledge, not coercion of the will in time.

name: Moral responsibility
definition: Being an appropriate object of praise or blame for an action.
precision_note: AQA specifies its conditions: free will, and understanding right from wrong.
attack_1: If every event is caused, no one could have acted otherwise and no one is blameworthy.
defence_1: Compatibilists redefine freedom as absence of external constraint rather than absence of causation.

name: Libertarianism
definition: Humans have genuine free will and determinism is false.
precision_note: Requires an agent who is genuinely undetermined. Critics ask how that differs from randomness.
attack_1: Redefining freedom is said to change the subject rather than answer the question.
defence_1: The freedom worth having is freedom from constraint, which is what praise and blame actually track.

name: Hard determinism
definition: Every event is caused, so free will is an illusion and no one is morally responsible.
precision_note: Follow it through to punishment: only deterrence and reform survive, never retribution.
attack_1: Desert-based punishment requires responsibility that determinism denies.
defence_1: Losing retribution is a gain, since deterrence and reform are the defensible aims anyway.

name: Compatibilism
definition: Determinism is true, but freedom as absence of constraint is compatible with it.
precision_note: Redefines freedom rather than defending it. Critics call this changing the subject.
attack_1: Redefining freedom is said to change the subject rather than answer the question.
defence_1: The freedom worth having is freedom from constraint, which is what praise and blame actually track.

name: Predestination
definition: God's eternal decree determining who is saved.
precision_note: Calvin's version threatens moral responsibility from a theological rather than scientific direction.
attack_1: Calvin's decree of election threatens responsibility from a theological direction.
defence_1: Predestination concerns God's eternal knowledge, not coercion of the will in time.

name: Retributive punishment
definition: Punishment deserved as a response to wrongdoing.
precision_note: Requires moral responsibility, so hard determinism rules it out.
attack_1: Desert-based punishment requires responsibility that determinism denies.
defence_1: Losing retribution is a gain, since deterrence and reform are the defensible aims anyway.

name: Reformative punishment
definition: Punishment aimed at changing the offender.
precision_note: Survives hard determinism, which is why determinists favour it.

name: Conscience
definition: The faculty or process by which a person judges the morality of their own acts.
precision_note: AQA wants religious and non-religious accounts contrasted, then applied to lying, promises and adultery.
attack_1: Jesus' teaching functions as an external authority that may override what conscience finds reasonable.
defence_1: If conscience is God's voice, it will not finally conflict with Jesus' teaching.

name: Conscientia
definition: Aquinas's term for reason applying moral principles to a particular case.
precision_note: Distinct from synderesis, which is the disposition. Conscientia can err.
presented_by: Thomas Aquinas (Dominican friar, c. 1225–1274) — "synderesis and conscientia"
attack_1: A fallible rational process and an infallible divine voice cannot both describe conscience.
defence_1: Conscience can be a rational faculty and still be God's voice, since reason is God-given.
defender_1: John Henry Newman (Cardinal, 1801–1890) — "the aboriginal Vicar of Christ"

name: Recta ratio
definition: Reason functioning correctly in moral judgement.

name: Super-ego
definition: Freud's internalised parental and social authority producing guilt.
precision_note: A wholly non-religious account: conscience is a psychological artefact, not a divine voice.

name: Id and ego
definition: Freud's other two components: instinctual drive and the reality-managing self.

name: Aboriginal Vicar of Christ
definition: Newman's description of conscience as the voice of God in the soul.
precision_note: The strongest religious account. Directly opposed to Freud — an easy paired paragraph.
presented_by: John Henry Newman (Cardinal, 1801–1890) — "the aboriginal Vicar of Christ"
attack_1: Freud (Neurologist, 1856–1939) argues conscience is the super-ego, an internalised parental and social authority.
defence_1: Butler (Bishop of Durham, 1692–1752) argues conscience carries an authority that a mere psychological artefact would not.
defender_1: Joseph Butler (Bishop of Durham, 1692–1752) — "conscience would govern the world"
attack_2: A fallible rational process and an infallible divine voice cannot both describe conscience.
defence_2: Conscience can be a rational faculty and still be God's voice, since reason is God-given.
defender_2: John Henry Newman (Cardinal, 1801–1890) — "the aboriginal Vicar of Christ"

name: Conscience as natural authority
definition: Butler's view that conscience naturally has authority over self-love and benevolence.
precision_note: Authority, not strength: it ought to govern even when it does not.

name: Sanctity of life
definition: The view that human life is intrinsically and equally valuable because it is God-given.
precision_note: Absolutist. Sits with NML; conflicts with quality-of-life reasoning.
attack_1: Intrinsic and conditional accounts of the value of life yield opposite verdicts on euthanasia.
defence_1: Sanctity of life already permits letting die, so it too weighs the condition of the life.
attack_2: An intrinsic and equal value cannot be traded off against aggregate welfare.
attack_3: Whether the embryo is a person is the question sanctity of life answers by definition and its critics answer by capacity.
attack_4: Treating an early embryo as equal to a person blocks research that would relieve enormous suffering.
defence_4: The image of God is not conferred by capacity, so potential is exactly the point.

name: Quality of life
definition: The view that the value of a life depends on its condition and prospects.
precision_note: Underpins most pro-euthanasia argument. Situation ethics and utilitarianism both use it.
attack_1: Intrinsic and conditional accounts of the value of life yield opposite verdicts on euthanasia.
defence_1: Sanctity of life already permits letting die, so it too weighs the condition of the life.

name: Personhood
definition: The question of which beings count morally and from when.
precision_note: The real crux of abortion and embryo research. Species membership, viability, or capacity.
attack_1: Whether the embryo is a person is the question sanctity of life answers by definition and its critics answer by capacity.

name: Viability
definition: The point at which a foetus could survive outside the womb.
precision_note: A legal line, not a moral argument. Say so if you use it.

name: Embryo research
definition: The use of human embryos in scientific study.

name: Cloning
definition: Producing a genetically identical organism.
precision_note: Distinguish therapeutic from reproductive cloning; the arguments differ.

name: Designer babies
definition: Selecting or editing embryos for chosen traits.

name: Abortion
definition: The deliberate termination of a pregnancy.
precision_note: Double effect is the NML route to permitting some cases. Use it rather than a flat prohibition.

name: Voluntary euthanasia
definition: Ending life at the sustained request of the person concerned.
precision_note: Distinguish from non-voluntary and involuntary, and active from passive. Precision earns marks here.

name: Assisted suicide
definition: Providing the means for a person to end their own life.

name: Active and passive euthanasia
definition: Actively causing death versus withholding treatment and allowing death.
precision_note: Whether the distinction is morally real is itself an exam question.
interacts_with: Voluntary euthanasia; Doctrine of double effect

name: Slippery slope argument
definition: Permitting one act will lead by degrees to unacceptable ones.
precision_note: Empirical, not logical. Attackable with evidence from jurisdictions that permit it.

name: Capital punishment
definition: Execution as a judicial penalty.
precision_note: Links to retributive versus reformative punishment in the free will topic.

name: Speciesism
definition: Singer's charge of unjustified bias toward one's own species.
precision_note: Modelled on racism and sexism. Sentience, not species, is his criterion.
attack_1: The dominion reading of Genesis is precisely what Singer (Moral philosopher, 1946–) identifies as unjustified bias.
defence_1: Stewardship grounds duties to animals without granting them equal standing.
attack_2: Both dominion and stewardship rank human interests above animal ones, which Singer (Moral philosopher, 1946–) calls unjustified bias.

name: Sentience
definition: The capacity to feel pleasure and pain.
precision_note: Singer's threshold for moral consideration.

name: Dominion and stewardship
definition: Genesis read either as licence to rule creation or as responsibility to care for it.
precision_note: The whole Christian animal ethics debate turns on which reading you take.
attack_1: The dominion reading of Genesis is precisely what Singer (Moral philosopher, 1946–) identifies as unjustified bias.
defence_1: Stewardship grounds duties to animals without granting them equal standing.
attack_2: Both dominion and stewardship rank human interests above animal ones, which Singer (Moral philosopher, 1946–) calls unjustified bias.
attack_3: Agape is directed at persons, so animal welfare enters only through its effect on people.

name: Intensive farming
definition: High-density livestock production.

name: Animal experimentation
definition: Using animals in scientific and medical procedures.

name: Blood sports
definition: Hunting or fighting animals for entertainment.
precision_note: The weakest case for permission on almost every theory — useful as a fixed point.

name: Xenotransplantation
definition: Transplanting animal organs into humans.

name: Imago Dei
definition: The doctrine that humans are made in the image of God.
precision_note: Grounds sanctity of life and human dignity. Hick uses image-and-likeness for soul-making.
attack_1: Grounding value in a religious doctrine gives no reason binding on those outside the tradition.
defence_1: A capacity criterion faces its own problem, since it excludes infants and the severely disabled.

name: Original sin
definition: The inherited corruption of human nature following the Fall.
precision_note: Augustine's version makes reason itself unreliable — relevant to natural theology.

name: The Fall
definition: The disobedience of Adam and Eve and its consequences.

name: Total depravity
definition: Calvin's view that every part of human nature is corrupted by sin.
precision_note: Undercuts the design and cosmological arguments: fallen reason cannot reach God unaided.

name: Grace
definition: God's unmerited favour toward humanity.

name: Justification by faith
definition: Being made right with God through faith rather than works.

name: Propositional revelation
definition: Revelation as the disclosure of true statements about God.
precision_note: Underwrites biblical authority and literalism. The target of Ayer's verification attack.
attack_1: Scriptural religious experiences can be explained as projections of psychological need.
defence_1: Credulity and testimony apply to biblical witnesses as they do to any other.
attack_2: Source and redaction criticism show the texts were composed, edited and shaped by communities.
defence_2: The Catholic position locates final authority in the interpreting Church rather than in the bare text.

name: Non-propositional revelation
definition: Revelation as God's self-disclosure in events, interpreted by the believer.
precision_note: Survives verification challenges better, but weakens claims to scriptural authority.

name: Biblical literalism
definition: The view that scripture is factually accurate in all it asserts.
precision_note: Depends on propositional revelation and on miracles being realist events.
interacts_with: Propositional revelation; Realist view of miracle
attack_1: Literalism makes the strongest possible factual claims and is therefore the most exposed to the verification challenge.
defence_1: The inspired-but-humanly-written position concedes historical conditioning while retaining authority.
attack_2: One holds that removing the myth removes the revelation; the other that keeping it obscures the revelation.
defence_2: Demythologising preserves the kerygma precisely by freeing it from a discredited world picture.
attack_3: Reading miracle narratives for their meaning removes any conflict with natural law, at the cost of the literal claim.
defence_3: If the miracles did not occur, the texts record what did not happen and their authority collapses.

name: Demythologisation
definition: Bultmann's programme of stripping mythological form to recover the existential message.
precision_note: A response to modern science, parallel to anti-realist accounts of miracle.
attack_1: One holds that removing the myth removes the revelation; the other that keeping it obscures the revelation.
defence_1: Demythologising preserves the kerygma precisely by freeing it from a discredited world picture.

name: Kerygma
definition: The essential proclamation of the Christian message.

name: Incarnation
definition: The doctrine that God became human in Jesus Christ.

name: Hypostatic union
definition: The union of divine and human natures in the one person of Christ.

name: Trinity
definition: One God in three persons.
precision_note: Dawkins's charge of incoherence is the standard philosophical attack.
attack_1: Three persons in one substance admits no empirical test, so on Ayer's account it is factually meaningless.
defence_1: Trinitarian language has its sense within Christian worship and creed, not within empirical enquiry.
attack_2: Dawkins (Evolutionary biologist, 1941–) argues the doctrine is incoherent and faith is belief without evidence.
defence_2: McGrath (Molecular biophysicist, 1953–) argues New Atheism overreaches its own evidential standards.

name: Atonement
definition: The reconciliation of God and humanity through Christ's death.

name: Eschatology
definition: Doctrine of the last things: death, judgement, heaven and hell.
precision_note: Hick's eschatological verification borrows directly from this.

name: Parousia
definition: The expected return of Christ.

name: Exclusivism
definition: Salvation is available only through explicit Christian faith.

name: Inclusivism
definition: Salvation comes through Christ but may reach those outside the visible Church.
precision_note: Rahner's anonymous Christians. Criticised as patronising by both sides.

name: Anonymous Christians
definition: Rahner's term for those saved by Christ without knowing it.
presented_by: Karl Rahner (Jesuit theologian, 1904–1984) — "anonymous Christians"
attack_1: Inclusivism annexes other faiths without taking their self-understanding seriously.
defence_1: Inclusivism takes other faiths seriously enough to say grace genuinely operates in them.

name: Religious pluralism
definition: All major religions are valid routes to the same ultimate reality.
precision_note: Hick's position, grounded in the Real. Accused of fitting no actual religion's self-understanding.
attack_1: Pluralism corresponds to no actual religion's own claims.
defence_1: Every tradition already reinterprets its own inherited claims, so pluralism asks nothing new.

name: The Real
definition: Hick's term for the noumenal ultimate behind all religious traditions.
precision_note: Kantian in structure: the Real in itself is never directly experienced.
presented_by: John Hick (Philosopher of religion, 1922–2012) — "the Real"

name: Feminist theology
definition: Theology that critiques and reconstructs Christianity in light of women's experience.
precision_note: Ruether reforms from within; Hampson concludes it cannot be reformed. That is the AQA contrast.
attack_1: Hampson (Post-Christian theologian, 1944–) argues reform from within has achieved little, since the tradition is irredeemably sexist.
defence_1: Ruether (Catholic feminist theologian, 1936–2022) points to real change: ordination, revised liturgy and the recovery of female imagery for God.
defender_1: Rosemary Radford Ruether (Catholic feminist theologian, 1936–2022) — "can a male saviour save women?"
attack_2: The largest Christian body still refuses women's ordination, so the movement's reach is limited.
defence_2: The scholarly shift that made 1 Timothy 2:8-15 readable as culturally conditioned affects all traditions.

name: Patriarchy
definition: Social and religious structures organised around male authority.

name: Androgynous Christ
definition: Ruether's claim that Christ transcends gender, so a male saviour can save women.
precision_note: Direct answer to 'can a male saviour save women?'
presented_by: Rosemary Radford Ruether (Catholic feminist theologian, 1936–2022) — "can a male saviour save women?"

name: Secularisation
definition: The declining social significance of religion.
attack_1: Relegating religion to the personal sphere restricts the public expression the right is meant to protect.

name: Christian monotheism
definition: One God, omnipotent creator and controller of all things, transcendent and unknowable, understood as Trinity.
precision_note: The doctrine process theology and Wiles both depart from. Name it when you say a view is unorthodox.
attack_1: A God who never acts particularly is hard to square with scripture and with prayer.
attack_2: A God who is neither omnipotent nor creator departs from the Christian doctrine of God.
defence_2: Process theology preserves God's goodness, which the creeds treat as more central than omnipotence.
attack_3: The design argument delivers at most a designer, not the Trinitarian creator of Christian doctrine.
defence_3: The arguments work cumulatively toward theism, with revelation supplying the specifically Christian content.
attack_4: Christian doctrine affirms all three of the propositions Mackie (Philosopher, 1917–1981) says cannot be held together.
defence_4: The free will defence shows the three propositions are not strictly inconsistent.
attack_5: A God who acts in history is presupposed by the creeds, so purely symbolic miracle undercuts the doctrine.
defence_5: Anti-realists argue the theological meaning was always the point, even for the earliest communities.

name: Inspiration of scripture
definition: The belief that the Bible is God-breathed while written by human authors.
precision_note: The spec's own wording: inspired by God but written by human beings. That middle position is neither literalism nor pure human authorship.

name: Biblical criticism
definition: The study of scripture as a historical document with sources, authors and contexts.
precision_note: Named in the spec as a nineteenth-century development that made challenging traditional readings possible.

name: Sola scriptura
definition: The Protestant principle that scripture is the sole final authority for doctrine.
precision_note: The direct contrast with the Catholic position, which the spec asks you to compare.
attack_1: One makes scripture self-interpreting; the other makes it interpretable only within the teaching office.
defence_1: Scripture has never in practice interpreted itself, as Protestant division demonstrates.

name: Magisterium
definition: The Catholic Church's authoritative teaching authority, held by pope and bishops.
precision_note: Not a rival to scripture but its authoritative interpreter. Saying Catholics value Church over Bible misstates the position.
attack_1: One makes scripture self-interpreting; the other makes it interpretable only within the teaching office.
defence_1: Scripture has never in practice interpreted itself, as Protestant division demonstrates.

name: Holy Tradition
definition: The living transmission of faith alongside and around scripture.
precision_note: Orthodox usage differs from Catholic: Tradition is the context of scripture rather than a second source.

name: Apostolic succession
definition: The unbroken line of ordination from the apostles to present bishops.
precision_note: Grounds the authority claim in Catholic and Orthodox tradition; rejected by congregational churches.

name: Priesthood of all believers
definition: The Reformation claim that every believer has direct access to God without priestly mediation.
precision_note: Underwrites both sola scriptura and congregational governance.

name: Authority of Jesus
definition: The status of Jesus' teaching, understood either as God's own authority or as that of an exemplary human.
precision_note: The spec ties this directly to Matthew 5:38-48 and to whether Jesus works as a role model.
supported_by: Analogy of proportion; Aboriginal Vicar of Christ
attack_1: The claim that Jesus is God cannot be verified or falsified, so on Ayer's account it asserts nothing.
defence_1: Hick (Philosopher of religion, 1922–2012) argues the claim is verifiable in principle after death.

name: Sermon on the Mount
definition: Jesus' teaching in Matthew 5-7, including non-retaliation and love of enemies.
precision_note: The spec names Matthew 5:38-48 specifically. Used for pacifism and for situation ethics.
attack_1: Jesus' teaching functions as an external authority that may override what conscience finds reasonable.
defence_1: If conscience is God's voice, it will not finally conflict with Jesus' teaching.

name: Transcendence
definition: God's existence beyond and independent of the created order.
precision_note: The spec pairs it with unknowable, which is what drives the religious language topic.

name: Creation ex nihilo
definition: The doctrine that God created without pre-existing material.
precision_note: Precisely what process theology denies, which is why Griffin's God is called not really God.
attack_1: Paley's designer arranges pre-existing material, whereas the Christian God creates from nothing.
defence_1: The analogy concerns the inference from contrivance to a contriver, not the mode of production.

name: God as Father
definition: The personal, paternal language the tradition uses of God.
precision_note: The spec asks about the challenge of anthropomorphic and gender specific language, so treat it as a problem, not a given.

name: Anthropomorphism
definition: Describing God in human terms and attributes.
precision_note: The pressure point between religious language and doctrine: too literal risks idolatry, too loose risks emptiness.
interacts_with: God as Father; Analogy of proportion

name: Objective immortality
definition: In process thought, survival as an everlasting memory within God rather than as a continuing self.
precision_note: Named in the spec. It is not personal survival, which is the standard objection to it.
attack_1: Process thought preserves the person only as everlasting memory in God, not as a continuing subject.
defence_1: Objective immortality abandons personal survival, which process thought regards as a lesser loss than divine coercion.

name: Particular judgement
definition: Judgement of the individual immediately at death.
precision_note: Distinguish from the general judgement at the parousia. Both are held together in Catholic teaching.
attack_1: Immediate judgement to heaven or hell leaves no room for the eventual salvation of all.
defence_1: Judgement can be remedial rather than final, so particular judgement and universal salvation are compatible.

name: Purgatory
definition: A state of purification after death before the beatific vision.
precision_note: Catholic; rejected by Protestants as unscriptural. A clean denominational contrast.
attack_1: No possible observation counts against claims about purgatory, so on Flew's account they assert nothing.
defence_1: Hick (Philosopher of religion, 1922–2012) argues post-mortem experience would settle such claims, so they remain factual.

name: Beatific vision
definition: The direct sight of God enjoyed by the saved.
precision_note: The goal purgatory prepares for. Useful for the meaning and purpose of life topic.

name: Universalism
definition: The view that all people are ultimately saved.
precision_note: Hick needs this for soul-making to be just, which links CH08 straight to PH05.
attack_1: Immediate judgement to heaven or hell leaves no room for the eventual salvation of all.
defence_1: Judgement can be remedial rather than final, so particular judgement and universal salvation are compatible.

name: Election
definition: God's choice of those to be saved.
precision_note: Calvin's unconditional election. The Arminian alternative makes election conditional on foreseen faith.

name: Justification by works
definition: The view that salvation involves human cooperation with grace, expressed in action.
precision_note: Named in the spec alongside justification by faith. Catholic teaching does not oppose faith and works.

name: Sanctification
definition: The process of being made holy after justification.
precision_note: Distinguishing justification from sanctification is the standard Protestant move and a precision point.

name: Just war theory
definition: Criteria under which war may be morally permissible.
precision_note: The spec names its application to weapons of mass destruction, which most criteria rule out.
interacts_with: Sanctity of life; Natural moral law

name: Weapons of mass destruction
definition: Nuclear, chemical and biological weapons.
precision_note: Named in the spec. Fails discrimination and proportionality under just war criteria.
interacts_with: Just war theory; Sanctity of life
attack_1: WMD fail the just war criteria of discrimination and proportionality, so no Christian use can be justified.
defence_1: Deterrence theorists argue possession prevents more deaths than it risks.
attack_2: Deliberately targeting non-combatants violates the sanctity of innocent life absolutely.
defence_2: Double effect might permit foreseen civilian deaths where they are not intended and not the means.

name: Creation care
definition: The view that environmental protection is a religious duty.
precision_note: The developed form of stewardship; links the incarnation to the value of the material world.

name: Believer's baptism
definition: Baptism given only on personal profession of faith, normally by full immersion.
precision_note: The Baptist position the spec contrasts with Catholic infant baptism.
attack_1: One requires a personal profession the infant cannot give; the other treats baptism as a gift preceding response.

name: Infant baptism
definition: Baptism administered to infants.
